policy_title: Expand Nuclear Power and Manage North Sea Oil and Gas Transition
stated: Labour will support new nuclear power stations like Sizewell C and Small Modular Reactors, and extend the lifetime of existing plants. They will not issue new licences for oil and gas exploration, but will not revoke existing licences, managing current North Sea fields for their lifespan to ensure a phased and responsible transition. The party will also maintain a strategic reserve of gas power stations.

source.quote: Labour will deliver the next generation of nuclear power. We will ensure the long-term security of the sector, extending the lifetime of existing plants, and we will get Hinkley Point C over the line. New nuclear power stations, such as Sizewell C, and Small Modular Reactors, will play an important role in helping the UK achieve energy security and clean power while securing thousands of good, skilled jobs. Labour will maintain a strategic reserve of gas power stations to guarantee security of supply. We will ensure a phased and responsible transition in the North Sea that recognises the proud history of our offshore industry and the brilliance of its workforce, particularly in Scotland and the North East of England, and the ongoing role of oil and gas in our energy mix. We will embrace the future of energy production and storage which will make use of existing offshore infrastructure and the skills of our offshore workforce. Labour will not revoke existing licences and we will partner with business and workers to manage our existing fields for the entirety of their lifespan. Crucially, oil and gas production in the North Sea will be with us for decades to come, and the North Sea will be managed in a way that does not jeopardise jobs. And our offshore workers will lead the world in the industries of the future. We will not issue new licences to explore new fields because they will not take a penny off bills, cannot make us energy secure, and will only accelerate the worsening climate crisis. In addition, we will not grant new coal licences and will ban fracking for good.

bearing_set.reason: No new oil/gas exploration licences directly constrains the domestic fossil-fuel supply pipeline, while nuclear expansion (Sizewell C, SMRs) provides low-carbon baseload — both bear materially on the UK's emissions trajectory.

Energy bills are an explicit O2 indicator; nuclear's high capital cost vs stable running cost, the degree of continued North Sea output, and reliance on a gas-power strategic reserve all plausibly affect household energy prices in the medium-to-long run.

Maintaining a strategic gas reserve, sustaining existing North Sea licences, and building nuclear baseload capacity all bear on energy-security resilience — explicitly an O5 indicator — reducing dependence on imported gas and external supply shocks.

The policy concretely creates and destroys specific categories of work: Sizewell C and SMRs generate large-scale skilled construction/operational employment while no-new-licences caps future North Sea exploration jobs; the explicitly 'managed transition' framing puts employment quality and security for energy-sector workers directly in scope.

Sizewell C and SMR deployment represent a multi-billion-pound industrial investment with productivity and competitiveness implications; energy reliability and long-run cost of electricity materially affect business investment and aggregate living standards.

Government financing of Sizewell C (initial public commitment already ~£1.7bn, with further equity/CfD exposure likely) is a material addition to the public balance sheet, historically subject to large cost overruns, constituting a non-negligible fiscal commitment.

membership_note: Policy spans energy-mix transition, environmental trajectory, household energy costs, workforce protection, and public financing of nuclear — five distinct fundamentals each with a concrete, non-negligible mechanism.
